profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a national energy systems lab where a near-final survey manuscript on smart grid cyber-physical system testbeds is being reviewed before submission to a power systems journal. The draft proposes a four-step taxonomy for classifying testbeds, summarizes 32 published platforms, and includes a comparison table plus design guidelines for future testbed builders. The agenda is to verify that the taxonomy and comparison framework are defensible for both power-systems and cybersecurity readers, resolve a few borderline classifications around hardware-in-the-loop and communication realism, and decide whether the manuscript can move to final revision and submission. The expected outcome is conditional approval of the paper structure with a short, concrete revision list.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Lead Author and Power Systems Research Scientist
members.expertise: smart grid testbeds, real-time digital simulation, controller-hardware-in-the-loop, power-hardware-in-the-loop, distributed energy resource integration
members.background: Lena leads a lab group that builds experimental distribution-grid platforms using RTDS and OPAL-RT environments, and she has published prior survey and benchmark papers on HIL-based validation of grid control architectures.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to validate the manuscript's current structure without reopening the literature coding or table schema, because the submission window is close and she believes the paper already captures the field's main architectural patterns.
hidden_assumptions: When reviewers call a survey 'comprehensive,' they mainly expect coverage of the major smart-grid domains, representative platform architectures, and recurring research goals rather than decision support for every specific downstream use case.

The taxonomy dimension labeled 'communication infrastructure' is supposed to capture communication technologies and protocol families at survey resolution, not every timing or deployment nuance unless the original paper centers on networking.

In this manuscript, 'HIL coverage' mainly means that controller-HIL and power-HIL families are visibly represented; communication hardware realism belongs under the communication dimension, not under HIL.

A manuscript described as needing a 'final revision' is one where category definitions, table structure, and inclusion logic are already settled and only targeted wording fixes or row-level checks remain.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: industrial control networks, substation communications, cyber-physical security evaluation, smart grid testbed instrumentation
members.background: Arjun came from an applied security center where he built attack-evaluation environments for substations and microgrids, with particular experience in IEC 61850 traffic capture, network emulation, and reproducing cyber-physical attack paths under realistic timing constraints.
members.private_state: He wants the survey to survive scrutiny from security-minded reviewers who care about whether a listed testbed can support meaningful vulnerability experiments, but he does not want to derail the paper this late by sounding as if he is asking for a structural rewrite.
hidden_assumptions: Calling the survey 'comprehensive' implies that a technically informed reader can tell, from the existing table and text, which testbeds are actually usable for different classes of cyber-physical security studies without repeatedly going back to the source papers.

The 'communication infrastructure' dimension naturally includes whether traffic runs through real switches, firewalls, or virtualized/emulated network layers, along with enough realism information to judge experiment validity.

When the manuscript says it has strong 'HIL representation,' that should include whether communication/network elements are physically in the loop for cyber experiments, not only whether controllers or power devices interact with a simulator.

A 'final revision' at this stage still includes rigorously verifying that borderline rows are classified in a way security reviewers would find technically accurate, even if no new columns or sections are added.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the survey should be 'comprehensive' and that the literature coverage looks 'broad enough.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes comprehensive means the manuscript captures the main smart-grid domains, representative testbed architectures, and enough literature to support a robust taxonomy and forward-looking design guidance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes comprehensive means the survey gives enough discriminating detail that readers can distinguish which platforms are suitable for concrete cyber-physical security evaluation scenarios, including borderline cases that test the taxonomy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a survey review, 'comprehensive' is a routine term of approval, and both participants can sincerely point to the same 32-paper corpus as evidence, so the different sufficiency standards stay latent.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to making sure the draft has strong 'HIL representation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the manuscript visibly covers the standard power-systems HIL families such as CHIL and PHIL, with a few hybrid examples where real controllers or power devices interact with a real-time simulated grid.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 hears HIL representation more broadly in a cyber-physical-security sense, where the strength of a HIL-heavy survey also depends on whether some reviewed platforms place real communication elements—such as protection relays, switches, firewalls, or protocol gateways—into the experimental loop rather than only simulating network behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use accepted domain language and both are talking about realism in 'the loop,' but because CHIL/PHIL are obviously valid HIL categories, neither notices that one person silently treats network hardware realism as part of what makes HIL coverage convincing.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of 'communication infrastructure' in the taxonomy
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the taxonomy already includes 'communication infrastructure' as one of the four steps.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this dimension includes items such as Ethernet, Wi-Fi, IEC 61850, DNP3, TCP/IP, and co-simulation middleware at a high descriptive level sufficient for a survey comparison table.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this dimension also covers whether the communication stack is physically deployed, virtualized, or emulated, whether segmentation is represented, and whether timing realism is present strongly enough to affect attack or control validity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both can point to the same column heading and the same protocol examples, the disagreement hides inside what each person takes to be the obvious contents of that heading rather than in the heading itself.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the paper should be ready after a 'final revision' this week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the final revision means polishing prose, tightening a few definitions, adding any missing citations, and making small row-level edits without revisiting the paper's settled comparison logic.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the final revision includes systematically rechecking ambiguous existing rows—especially the security-relevant classifications around HIL and communication realism—to make sure the current table is technically defensible, even without changing its structure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'final revision' comfortably covers both light editorial work and targeted verification, so each hears a reasonable late-stage workload and no one feels the need to spell out the exact review procedure.

The paper already captures the main architectural patterns across the 32 papers. What I need from this meeting is confirmation that the taxonomy and comparison framework stand, and that a final revision this week means polishing language, fixing a few row-level issues, and submitting on schedule.
